introduction: On this Sunday, the readings speak of small beginnings and great growth. Ezekiel sees God plant a tender shoot that becomes a noble cedar. Jesus compares the Kingdom of God to seed that grows by itself while the farmer sleeps, and to the tiny mustard seed that becomes a large plant. Paul reminds us that we walk by faith, not by sight. Let us trust the quiet growth of God's Kingdom.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God makes the small seed grow. Let us bring our prayers to him with confidence.
intentions: For the Church: that she may sow the word of God patiently and trust God to give the growth. Let us pray to the Lord.
For parents, teachers and catechists: that they may not lose heart when they cannot yet see the fruit of their work. Let us pray to the Lord.
For farmers and all who work the land: that their harvests may be good and their labor fairly rewarded. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel small or insignificant: that they may know that God can do great things through them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may walk by faith and not by sight, and please the Lord in all we do. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you make the smallest seed grow into a great tree. Help us to sow your word with faith and to wait for your harvest with patience. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The seed grows by itself
reflection.body:
Ezekiel speaks to a people in exile who have lost everything. God promises that he will take a tender shoot from the top of the cedar and plant it on a high mountain, where "it will produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a good cedar." Birds of every kind will nest in it. God is the one who acts: "I, the LORD, have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree."

Jesus tells two short parables about seeds. In the first, a man scatters seed, then goes about his life, "and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn't know how." Growth is God's work, not ours. We sow; God gives the increase.

In the second, the mustard seed, tiny when sown, "grows up and becomes greater than all the herbs, and puts out great branches, so that the birds of the sky can lodge under its shadow." The Kingdom of God often begins in ways that look insignificant: a word, a prayer, a small kindness.

This is a great comfort for anyone who works for God and sees little result: parents praying for their children, catechists, priests, people who have shared their faith with a friend. The seed is growing even when we cannot see it.

Paul puts it simply: "we walk by faith, not by sight." And he gives us our aim: "whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him."

This week, think of one person you have been praying for or trying to help, and entrust them again to God, who makes things grow. Then sow one more small seed: a word of encouragement, a prayer, an invitation.
